operationalization: Map crooked-talon birds to living raptors and owls, then compare clutch-size distributions with the kestrel. The claim stands if kestrels have the highest clutch sizes in that set and commonly reach four or more eggs, and fails if several other raptors match or exceed them or if kestrels rarely reach four.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: species-level clutch size for raptors, owls and the common kestrel

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size and related reproductive traits for the same species

obstacles: Crooked talons need an explicit taxon list, including whether owls belong.
Unprolific needs a numeric clutch-size cutoff.
rationale: Clutch size is a standard field in open avian life-history tables, with broad coverage of hawks, falcons and owls. A ranking of those clutch sizes directly tests both the general scarcity of eggs and the kestrel exception. Species limits and the word unprolific are the main judgments a pre-registered cutoff has to fix.

operationalization: Compare yolk mass as a fraction of egg contents, and albumen fraction, between birds that nest or feed in marshes and rivers and birds that do not, within developmental mode. A higher yolk fraction and lower albumen fraction in the waterbirds would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad: bird egg composition and shape
candidate_datasets.role: shell, yolk and albumen proportions linked to egg shape for a comparative bird sample

candidate_datasets.name: Deeming egg-composition compilation
candidate_datasets.role: yolk and albumen masses for 279 bird species across 21 orders

obstacles: Waterbirds are mostly precocial, so habitat is confounded with hatchling maturity.
Marsh and river species are a subset of the published composition tables.
rationale: Published compilations record yolk and albumen masses for hundreds of species, so the proportion itself is measurable. Habitat and developmental mode move together, and a test that does not separate them cannot tell a waterbird effect from the known precocial-yolk pattern. The comparison is feasible for the species already measured and thin outside that sample.

operationalization: On domestic-hen eggs, relate a shape index (length-to-breadth and bluntness of the narrow end), measured before incubation, to hatchling sex, with hen and egg mass as covariates. A repeatable excess of females from long pointed eggs and males from rounder eggs would support the claim.
obstacles: Paired egg-shape and sex-at-hatch records are scattered in small poultry trials.
No open multi-flock table covers the rule as stated.
rationale: Egg shape and hatchling sex are both measurable, and a pre-registered regression would discriminate the rule from chance. The trials that exist are small, dispersed and mostly limited to the domestic hen, so they can probe the claim without covering it at the scale of a life-history database. A decisive test needs those records compiled or collected again.

operationalization: In flocks of hens and geese known never to have been with a male, record whether they lay eggs and whether those eggs are infertile. Laying by never-mated females would refute the view that wind-eggs are leftovers of earlier copulation.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of domestic fowl and goose reproduction, including unfertilized laying

obstacles: Quantitative virgin-flock trials sit in poultry papers rather than a trait table.
Coverage is much stronger for the hen than for the goose, partridge or pigeon.
rationale: The decision criterion is direct: females with no mating history either lay infertile eggs or they do not. Poultry husbandry and anatomical accounts document that outcome for the domestic hen, with thinner published coverage for geese and the other birds named alongside them. The rival residue-of-copulation account is what those virgin layings discriminate.

operationalization: Regress incubation length, and where recorded the interval from ovulation or mating to laying, on adult body mass across birds, with phylogeny controlled. A positive size relationship for both intervals would support the claim; a flat incubation relationship would refute that half.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and incubation duration across birds

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: incubation and body-mass records for the same comparison

obstacles: Time to form the egg after copulation is sparsely recorded.
Body size is confounded with developmental mode and clutch size.
rationale: Incubation duration and adult mass are standard open variables, so the hatching half of the claim can be fit directly. The time required to form the egg is a different interval and is mostly in species studies, so the compound claim is only partly covered. Phylogenetic controls are routine and do not remove that gap.

operationalization: Using staged chick embryos, record when a beating heart and paired vitelline vessels first appear relative to other organs. The claim stands if that stage is a small blood-red beating heart with two blood-filled vessels leaving it, and fails if the heart is not yet beating when it becomes visible or the vessel pattern differs.

candidate_datasets.name: eChickAtlas
candidate_datasets.role: staged chick anatomy through the period of heart-tube and vessel formation

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA chicken-embryo gene-expression atlas
candidate_datasets.role: stage and anatomical location of early heart development in the chick

obstacles: Open atlases are built on the domestic chick, with other birds inferred.
Which structure counts as first is a staging judgment.
rationale: Hamburger-Hamilton staging and public chick atlases show the heart tube and the early vessels at known stages. A small team can score those images against the beating speck and the two vessels without new experiments. Coverage is excellent for the hen's egg, which is the observation Aristotle reports.

operationalization: In staged bird embryos, locate the embryo relative to yolk and albumen and trace whether nutrients reach it through the yolk-sac stalk. Yolk-sac nutrition would support the nourishment clause; a blastoderm seated on the yolk would undermine the claim that the life of the chick lies in the white.

candidate_datasets.name: eChickAtlas
candidate_datasets.role: position of the chick embryo relative to yolk and extraembryonic membranes

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA chicken-embryo gene-expression atlas
candidate_datasets.role: early embryonic tissues at the yolk surface and in the yolk sac

obstacles: Life-element is not a measured variable.
Albumen and yolk are both nutritive, so the exclusive wording needs a pre-set criterion.
rationale: Atlases can show where the embryo sits and that a yolk-sac circulation supplies it, which is the observable nutrition clause. The further claim that the principle of life lies in the white is only partly fixed by that anatomy, because both egg fractions contribute water, protein or lipid. The nutrition path is testable now; the life-element wording stays interpretive.

operationalization: Take age at first reproduction for birds and compute the share with that age under one year. The claim stands if that share is very small under a pre-registered cutoff, and fails if a large fraction of species, especially small passerines, breed in year one.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: age at first reproduction across birds

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: female and male age at sexual maturity for birds

obstacles: Very few needs a numeric threshold.
Age at maturity is an imperfect stand-in for age at first successful breeding.
rationale: Age at first reproduction is tabulated for thousands of bird species. The distribution either concentrates above one year or it does not, which is enough to confirm or refute a claim that very few birds breed in their first year. Missing species and the maturity proxy limit precision, and they leave the direction of the result readable.

operationalization: After a defined injury that destroys the eye of nestling barn swallows, follow whether the eye regenerates and whether vision returns. Recovery of sight would support the claim; permanent blindness in a pre-registered sample would refute it.
obstacles: No public experimental series records this injury in Hirundo rustica.
General reviews of vertebrate regeneration do not replace a swallow outcome.
rationale: The prediction is a clear recovery-or-not endpoint. Published regeneration summaries do not contain a swallow puncture series with sample size, follow-up and a vision measure. Resolving the claim requires that experiment or an equivalent unpublished record brought into the open.

operationalization: For Aquila species, summarize clutch size, number hatched, incubation length and the cause of brood reduction. Support requires modal clutch near three, usual brood of two, incubation near 30 days, and the parent actively expelling a chick; siblicide or starvation without expulsion would fail that clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size and incubation duration for eagle species

candidate_datasets.name: British Trust for Ornithology
candidate_datasets.role: nest records for clutch, hatch and incubation in monitored raptors

obstacles: Aquila species differ in clutch size and incubation.
Parental expulsion is rarely separated from siblicide in nest records.
rationale: Clutch size and incubation length for eagles are in open life-history tables and nest schemes, so those numbers can be checked now. Active expulsion by the mother is a behavioral detail that standard tables do not code, and brood reduction in eagles is often sibling aggression. The numerical clauses are testable; the expulsion clause needs case narratives.

operationalization: Compare foot and beak measurements and phylogenetic placement of Cuculus canorus with Accipiter hawks, and compile records of hawks killing cuckoos. Separate ancestry plus hawk-like talons absent in the cuckoo, or predation of cuckoos by hawks, would refute the transformed-hawk account.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic separation of cuckoos and hawks

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: beak, tarsus and body-size measurements for cuckoos and hawks

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits
candidate_datasets.role: diet and foraging records bearing on hawk predation

obstacles: Talon curvature is only partly captured by tarsus length.
Predation events are rarer in trait tables than in species monographs.
rationale: Aristotle's criteria are anatomical difference and cross-species predation, both of which public phylogenies and morphological tables address. Cuckoos and hawks are not close relatives, and foot and bill measurements quantify the talon and head contrast he uses. Predation records add a behavioral check and are less complete than the tree.

operationalization: For the common cuckoo, score nest-building, eggs per host nest, removal or eating of host eggs, and whether the host incubates and feeds the young. The claim fails if common cuckoos regularly build and incubate, lay large clutches in their own nests, or leave the host's eggs intact as the usual pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Field Museum brood-parasite host lists
candidate_datasets.role: compiled host records for Old World cuckoos, including the common cuckoo

candidate_datasets.name: British Trust for Ornithology
candidate_datasets.role: nest records of cuckoo eggs in host nests in Britain

obstacles: Host lists record the foster species more often than whether the female ate the host eggs.
Some other cuckoo species are not parasitic, so the species map must stay on Cuculus canorus.
rationale: Brood parasitism of the common cuckoo is documented in an open host list and in long-running nest records. Those sources show laying in other birds' nests and rearing by the host. Whether the adult eats the host clutch, rather than removing an egg while the chick later ejects the rest, is a finer point inside species studies.

operationalization: Compare testis mass, scaled by body mass, in and out of the breeding season for male birds, with the domestic cock and male partridge included. Seasonal enlargement, largest in those two, would support the claim; no seasonal change would refute it.
obstacles: Seasonal testis size is in endocrinology papers, not a life-history column.
Salacious is not an independent measured trait.
rationale: Testis mass by season is a standard measurement, and published series exist for poultry, galliforms and many passerines. They are not gathered into one open table, so a test means compiling those series for a pre-chosen species list. The within-male seasonal contrast is clean once the numbers are in hand; ranking salaciousness is the softer clause.

operationalization: Code reproductive mode for cartilaginous fishes and for bony fishes, and check Lophius separately. The claim stands only if cartilaginous fishes are viviparous after internal eggs, other fishes are oviparous, and the fishing-frog is the stated exception.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for bony fishes and for Lophius

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of sharks, rays and chimaeras, including egg-laying and live-bearing

obstacles: Aristotle's cartilaginous group includes the fishing-frog, which is a bony fish.
Skates are cartilaginous and many lay eggs, so the universal needs that exception counted.
rationale: Reproductive mode is a core field in FishBase and Sharkipedia, covering thousands of fishes and the living sharks and rays. Those tables can confirm or refute universal viviparity of cartilaginous fishes, universal oviparity of the rest, and the status of Lophius. The remaining care is mapping his group names onto those taxa.

operationalization: For Mustelus mustelus, record whether embryos attach to the uterine wall by a cord after yolk stores decline, and whether a chorion and extraembryonic membranes are present. A yolk-sac placenta with those membranes would support the claim; yolk dependence until birth without a uterine cord would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode, including placental viviparity, for smooth-hounds

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and embryo notes for Mustelus

obstacles: Several Mustelus species differ in placental detail.
Chorion and membrane histology sit in anatomical papers more than in the trait table.
rationale: Smooth-hound reproductive mode, including placental attachment, is recorded in open elasmobranch trait data and species accounts. That is enough to test the cord-to-the-womb claim for the species usually identified with Aristotle's smooth shark. Fine structure of the chorion still has to be read from the anatomical descriptions those databases cite.

operationalization: Compare parturition locations with offshore habitat for sharks and rays, and test whether nursery sites are warmer and have fewer predators than adjacent adult habitat. Inshore pupping would support the movement clause; no temperature or predator difference would leave the stated purpose unsupported.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: parturition and nursery-related life-history traits for sharks and rays

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: coastal versus offshore occurrence of sharks and rays

obstacles: For the sake of warmth and protection is not fixed by location alone.
Many pelagic species pup far from shore.
rationale: Nursery use and coastal occurrence can be scored for a substantial set of sharks and rays. The purpose clause needs a contrast of temperature and predation that existing occurrence tables only partly supply, and food or current cues fit the same inshore pattern. The movement is partly testable; the final cause is weakly separated from rivals.

operationalization: Tally documented hybrid pairings among fishes against the number of species pairs with intensive breeding studies. The general rule stands if hybrids are rare relative to opportunity, and fails if interspecific pairing is common in well-studied groups.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts and reproductive notes that record fish hybrids

obstacles: Kind can mean species or a broader sort of fish.
Hybrid lists are biased toward freshwater fishes that people breed.
rationale: FishBase and the papers behind it record many hybrids, which is enough to test a general ban on cross-kind pairing in well-studied families. Absence of a hybrid record is weak evidence that pairing never occurs, and marine species are poorly covered. The rule can be assessed as a frequency in the compiled subset, not as a universal negative.

operationalization: For every living cetacean, record reproductive mode and whether an egg stage is carried. Universal live birth with no egg-laying would support the claim; any egg-laying cetacean would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and gestation for cetacean species

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of cetacean reproduction

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for dolphins, porpoises and whales

obstacles: Fossil stem cetaceans are outside the living animals the claim describes.
rationale: Live birth versus eggs is recorded for the living whales, dolphins and porpoises in mammal trait tables and species accounts. The set is small enough to check species by species. A single egg-laying cetacean would refute the universal claim, and the open accounts agree on the variable that would show it.

operationalization: For dolphins and porpoises, record presence of mammary glands, milk and a nursing period. Nursing of the young would support the claim; absence of lactation would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: weaning age as evidence of lactation in dolphins and porpoises

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of nursing in dolphin and porpoise species

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: lactation and parental care for Delphinidae and Phocoenidae

obstacles: Weaning age is a proxy for milk transfer when milk composition itself is untabulated.
rationale: Lactation and a weaning period are standard entries for dolphins and porpoises. Species accounts describe nursing directly, and trait tables record weaning age across the groups. The claim is a presence statement with a small, well-covered taxon list.

operationalization: Code reproductive mode for scaled teleosts, for eel-like slippery fishes, and for Anguilla. The claim stands if the scaled and slippery species are oviparous and eels are not; live-bearing scaled fishes, or oviparous eels, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for bony fishes, including eels and mullets

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: modern names for the basse, mullet, etelis and eel

obstacles: Scaly and smooth are ancient groupings, not taxa.
The eel exception is itself an empirical clause that the life cycle can fail.
rationale: FishBase codes oviparity and live-bearing across bony fishes, including the named mullets, basses and the European eel. That is enough to test the universals once a taxon map is fixed. The map from scaly and smooth to modern groups is the main limit, because different maps change which exceptions count.

operationalization: For each candidate identification of erythrinus and channa, tally the sex ratio and the fraction of adults carrying eggs. The claim stands if samples contain only egg-bearing fish; a regular class of fish without eggs would refute it for that identification.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sex strategy and reproductive state for candidate serranids and seabreams

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: candidate scientific names for channa and erythrinus

obstacles: Channa and erythrinus have competing modern identifications.
Hermaphrodite labels are not the same as a catch composition of all-pregnant fish.
rationale: If the names are serranids or a protogynous seabream, FishBase records sex strategy and spawning biology for those candidates. Simultaneous hermaphroditism would explain catches that all contain eggs, and it is not the same measurement as Aristotle's never caught except pregnant. Because the Greek names map in more than one way, the result can differ by identification.

operationalization: For externally fertilizing fishes, compare development of eggs with and without sperm exposure. Development restricted to sperm-exposed eggs would support the claim; regular development of unexposed eggs, or an internal-fertilization life cycle, would limit or refute the universal wording.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fertilization mode and reproductive mode across oviparous fishes

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish fertilization assays in which eggs develop only after sperm exposure

obstacles: Many oviparous fishes fertilize internally, outside the milt-over-eggs picture.
Trial data are dense for aquaculture and model species and thin elsewhere.
rationale: Fertilization mode is coded broadly, and experimental systems such as zebrafish measure development with and without sperm. Those data test the mechanism for external fertilizers. They do not cover every oviparous fish, and internal fertilizers are a different procedure, so the universal scope stays partly open.

operationalization: Compare spawning and larval locations of marine fishes with offshore waters, and test whether inshore sites are warmer, richer in food and lower in large predators. A majority of species spawning offshore, or no inshore advantage on those three measures, would undermine the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: spawning habitat and fecundity for marine fishes

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence of fish eggs and larvae inshore and offshore

obstacles: Eels, tunas and many others spawn in the open sea.
Warmth, food and protection are confounded reasons for the same coastal pattern.
rationale: Spawning habitat and larval occurrences can show how often marine fishes use the shore. The three benefits Aristotle names are only partly measured in those tables, and several rival reasons predict the same shift inshore. The location claim is testable for well-known species; the purpose claim is not cleanly separated.

operationalization: In normal tables for oviparous fishes, order the first visible appearance of eyes against other organs, and compare that sequence with insect larvae that differentiate the posterior end first. Eyes among the first large external organs would support the fish clause; an earlier non-eye organ as the rule would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish staging series with the timing of optic vesicle and eye formation

obstacles: Staging coverage is deep for zebrafish and a few other models, not for fishes generally.
First visible organ depends on the imaging method.
rationale: Zebrafish and a handful of other fishes have public stage series in which eye formation can be ordered against somites, brain and heart. That tests the claim for those species and against grub-like posterior-first development. It does not yet cover oviparous fishes as a whole.

operationalization: For Silurus aristotelis, measure days of male attendance at the egg mass, whether the female leaves after spawning, and egg developmental time relative to other freshwater fishes. A male guard period of about 40 to 50 days with female departure would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: parental care and reproductive notes for Silurus aristotelis and related catfishes

obstacles: Guard duration is rarely a database field and rests on a few field studies.
Developmental time depends on temperature.
rationale: FishBase records parental care for Aristotle's catfish and its relatives, which tests male guarding and female departure at a coarse level. The specific 40-to-50-day watch and the claim of exceptionally slow development sit in a small field literature, not in a multi-population table. The species identification itself is unusually secure.

operationalization: Code migration direction for Mugilidae and for Anguilla anguilla between sea and rivers or marshes. The claim stands if mullets move from the sea into brackish or fresh water and eels leave rivers and marshes for the sea to spawn.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: migration type for grey mullets and the European eel

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: European eel assessments of the downstream spawning migration

obstacles: Several mullet species differ in how far they penetrate fresh water.
Aristotle's mullet is a mugilid group, not one modern species.
rationale: FishBase codes catadromy and related movements for the European eel and for grey mullets, and ICES assessments document the eel's migration to sea. Direction of travel is the whole empirical content. Species-level differences among mullets affect how far inland they go, not the sea-to-lagoon direction the claim states.

operationalization: Identify the small fry Aristotle derives from mud or sand and determine whether they hatch from eggs of known parents and later grow and reproduce. A closed life cycle from eggs would refute spontaneous origin; fry that never recruit would be required for the sterility clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle and early-stage records for candidate anchovies, gobies and mullets

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence records of larval fishes in coastal shallows

obstacles: Aphya and the mullet near Cnidos are insecurely identified.
Cannot grow or reproduce needs cohort data, not just a species name.
rationale: Once a fry type is identified, FishBase life-cycle records test whether it comes from eggs and whether adults reproduce. That is the observable content of a spontaneous-generation claim. The ancient fry names do not map cleanly, so the same data can refute the claim for a candidate species and still miss the population he saw.

operationalization: Examine gonads of European eels across the yellow and silver stages for milt, eggs and genital ducts. Any eel with identifiable milt, roe or reproductive passages would refute the universal negative.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode, maturity and gonad notes for Anguilla anguilla

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: assessments and cited studies of silver-eel maturation and spawning

obstacles: Yellow eels in rivers have undeveloped gonads, so a river-only sample repeats Aristotle's observation.
Fully ripe oceanic adults remain rarely sampled.
rationale: The claim is a universal negative about milt, spawn and ducts. Silver-eel studies and FishBase reproductive records document developing gonads and an oviparous life cycle, which is the observation that would refute it. A sample restricted to feeding-stage river eels would miss that stage, so the test has to include maturing migrants.

operationalization: Trace European eel early life from supposed mud worms versus from eggs and leptocephalus larvae. Origin from a identified worm in mud would support the claim; a life cycle through marine larvae and eggs would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: life cycle of Anguilla anguilla from leptocephalus to spawning adult

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: stock biology of the oceanic spawning migration

obstacles: The worm called earth's guts has no secure modern species name.
The eel life cycle does not depend on naming that worm.
rationale: The observable prediction is that eels arise from worms generated in mud. The European eel life cycle, from leptocephalus to silver eel and oceanic spawning, is documented in FishBase and in the assessment literature. That life cycle is a direct alternative to origin from earth's guts, whether or not the worm name can be matched.

operationalization: Collect incubation or gestation lengths in days for fishes and test whether every value is at most 30 and divisible by 7. Any well-measured duration outside that set refutes the universal rule.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: incubation and gestation lengths for bony and cartilaginous fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for sharks and rays

obstacles: Gestation may mean pregnancy or egg incubation.
Development time changes with temperature, and many records are ranges.
rationale: Day counts of incubation and gestation are widespread in FishBase and Sharkipedia. A rule that every duration is a multiple of seven and no longer than 30 days fails as soon as reliable counts fall elsewhere, which those tables contain. Temperature ranges make single-day precision uneven, and they do not rescue a seven-day numerology if the ranges themselves miss those values.

operationalization: Compare annual fecundity or litter size, offspring size and, where measured, juvenile mortality between cartilaginous fishes and other fishes. Lower fecundity and higher early survival in selachians would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity, offspring size and reproductive mode across fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: litter size, offspring size and natural mortality for sharks and rays

obstacles: Juvenile survival is far sparser than litter size.
Viviparity and shared ancestry confound a raw selachian-versus-bony contrast.
rationale: Litter size and offspring size are tabulated well enough to test the fecundity contrast and the claim that the young are large. Survival is the clause that existing data cover only in part: natural-mortality estimates exist for some sharks and are not comparable across fishes generally. Body size and reproductive mode have to be controlled before the contrast is read as a selachian effect.

operationalization: Score aggression by sex and reproductive state for the named mammals, with females compared just after birth and males compared in rut versus other seasons. Higher female aggression postpartum and higher male aggression in rut would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: behavioral accounts of rut and maternal aggression in the named mammals

obstacles: Bad-tempered is not a standard ethogram variable.
Quantitative series cover livestock and deer far better than bear, lion or camel.
rationale: Rut aggression and postpartum defense are described for several of the named species in natural-history accounts and livestock studies. They are not in a comparative behavior table with a common scale, so the test is a compilation for a subset. The universal timing rule across horse, boar, bull, ram, camel, bear, wolf, lion and dog is wider than those series.

operationalization: Compare birth or hatching month with the month when juveniles become independent, against local resource or temperature peaks. A match between rearing time and a pre-registered favorable season would support the observable pattern; the adapted-so-as wording needs that match to beat alternative timings.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: breeding and rearing traits across amniotes

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: age at maturity and weaning as rearing-time measures

obstacles: Convenient season and adapted so as are loose.
Birth month and resource peaks are often missing from the trait tables.
rationale: Life-history tables record rearing periods more often than the seasonal food peak those periods are supposed to meet. Where both exist, alignment can be tested for a subset of species. Many different schedules can be called convenient, and phylogeny and body size predict seasonality without a separate adaptive test, so discrimination stays weak.

operationalization: Link wind direction at mating of sheep and goats to the sex of the offspring, with season and breed controlled. A higher male fraction after north winds and a higher female fraction after south winds would support the claim.
obstacles: No public table pairs wind direction at conception with lamb or kid sex.
Separate weather archives and flock books are not linked.
rationale: The prediction is specific enough to test with flock books and wind records. Those two data streams are not published as a joined dataset, and sex-ratio studies of sheep do not carry wind direction. Confirming or refuting the rule requires that linkage, which is not available now.

operationalization: Compare survival curves of male and female horses and of stable-kept versus herd-kept horses, then test whether mating load explains the male deficit after age and management are controlled. Shorter male life confined to breeding stallions, plus longer stable life, would support both clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity records and sources for the horse

obstacles: AnAge does not split horse lifespan by sex or by stable versus herd.
Sexual service is confounded with other sex differences and with workload.
rationale: A species-level longevity record exists, and veterinary cohorts in the literature discuss sex and management. They are not an open survival table with mating history, so the causal clause cannot be separated from other differences between stallions and mares. Stable-versus-troop longevity is similarly scattered.

operationalization: Compare mule gestation (jack × mare) and hinny gestation (stallion × jenny) with horse and donkey gestations, and score foal size and morphology against sire and dam. Gestation matching the sire's species, and foals closer to the dam, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation lengths of horse and donkey as the parental baselines

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of horse, donkey and mule reproduction

obstacles: Hybrid gestations are in veterinary case series, not in AnAge.
Resemblance in looks and vigour needs a pre-set morphometric score.
rationale: Horse and donkey gestation lengths are tabulated, which supplies the two parental baselines. Mule and hinny gestations and parent-offspring resemblance are in case series rather than a public hybrid table, so both clauses can be examined only after a compilation. The comparison itself is discriminating once those lengths and measurements are aligned.

operationalization: Compile veterinary cases of female mules with confirmed pregnancy and record whether any reached parturition. Pregnancies that end without birth fit the stated case; live births limit a reading on which pregnancy never continues to birth.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive accounts of mules, including sterility and rare fertility reports

obstacles: The sentence is one historical case, which modern series do not identify.
Rare live mule births and failed pregnancies are both reported, so the universal reading and the existential reading diverge.
rationale: Species accounts and case reports document mule pregnancy and the usual failure to produce a foal, which is the general phenomenon behind the sentence. They do not identify Aristotle's particular mule. Reading the claim as never carried to birth is testable in those reports; reading it as a single ancient anecdote is not.

operationalization: Place red-deer gestation, juvenile growth and maximum longevity on the mammalian life-history plane, and test whether short gestation and fast maturity predict short maximum lifespan. Deer longevity inside the ordinary mammalian range, rather than a multi-century life, would support the negative conclusion about fabulous ages.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation, age at maturity and maximum longevity for deer and other mammals

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length, body mass and life-history traits for the same comparison

obstacles: Extreme longevity has no numeric cutoff in the text.
Maximum-longevity records are often from captivity.
rationale: Gestation, growth schedule and longevity for red deer and for mammals at large are in open databases. Those fields test both the deer facts Aristotle uses and the inference that short gestation and fast growth count against extreme age. The correlation has exceptions, so it supports a comparative argument rather than a deduction that every short-gestation mammal is short-lived.

operationalization: Rank mammals by neonate mass divided by adult female mass, and compare absolute neonate mass of the brown bear with mouse and weasel masses. The claim also requires newborn bears to be hairless, blind and incompletely formed; mass ranks and neonatal descriptions can each fail separately.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: neonatal and adult body mass across mammals, including bears

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: birth weight and adult weight for bears, mice and mustelids

obstacles: Marsupials have still smaller neonate-to-mother ratios if they are included.
Hair, vision and limb completeness are in species accounts rather than the mass tables.
rationale: Neonate and adult masses are standard mammal-trait fields, so the relative-size ranking and the mouse-to-weasel absolute comparison can be computed directly. Altricial features of bear cubs are described in the same literature the databases draw on. Whether bears are the smallest of all animals depends on including marsupials, which a pre-registered taxon scope has to state.

operationalization: Dissect or image male and female striped hyenas and score whether each sex has one functional genital opening plus a blind look-alike, or two functional sets of organs. Functional organs of both sexes in every individual would refute Aristotle's denial of hermaphroditism.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical and reproductive accounts of striped and spotted hyenas

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: open specimen media for carnivoran anatomy, including hyenas where deposited

obstacles: Striped and spotted hyenas differ in the female genitalia.
The blind part has to be matched to a pseudopenis, pouch or duct before the description can pass or fail.
rationale: Hyena reproductive anatomy is described in detail in open species accounts and anatomical papers, which is enough to test true hermaphroditism against a single functional sex. Specimen repositories add images where hyenas have been deposited, with uneven coverage. The striped hyena, the likely referent, does not match the spotted hyena's extreme female masculinization, so the species map changes the anatomical target.

operationalization: For the European hare, compile litters per year, breeding months, gestation and evidence of a second conception during pregnancy. Year-round breeding with a litter every month and superfetation would support the claim; a seasonal schedule or fewer than about twelve litters a year would fail the frequency clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litters per year, litter size and gestation for Lepus europaeus

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive schedule and litter frequency for hares

obstacles: Superfetation is not a column in the trait tables.
Breeding season length changes with latitude.
rationale: Litters per year and gestation are tabulated and can refute a literal birth every month. Superfetation in the European hare is reported in reproductive studies that are not in those tables, so that clause needs the primary papers. Latitude shifts the breeding season, which matters for the all-seasons wording.

operationalization: Rank mammals and other small vertebrates by litter size and by litters per year, or by their product, and place mice on that ranking. The claim stands if mice are at the extreme of the pre-registered metric and fails if other species clearly exceed them.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size, litters per year and interbirth interval across mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and reproductive frequency, including mice and other rodents

obstacles: Most prolific can mean litter size, frequency or annual offspring.
Captive rodents inflate reproductive output relative to wild mice.
rationale: Litter size and reproductive frequency are filled widely enough to rank mice against other mammals. That ranking confirms or refutes an extremal claim once the metric is fixed in advance. Mice sit near the top on several metrics, and other rodents can outrank them, which is a result the same tables can show.

operationalization: Estimate the age at which boys first produce semen and the age at which pubic hair reaches a defined stage, in more than one population. The claim stands if both cluster near fourteen, and fails if the central ages lie well away from fourteen or the two events do not coincide.

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: age at sexual debut in national surveys, a proxy rather than spermarche or pubic-hair stage

obstacles: Open survey data record sexual debut more often than first semen or Tanner pubic hair.
Age at puberty has shifted across populations and centuries.
rationale: Semenarche and pubic-hair stage are measured in pediatric cohorts, and those cohorts are scattered rather than released as one open table. Demographic surveys supply age at sexual debut, which is a later and different event. The age-fourteen claim can be probed with the published series and is not settled by the survey proxy alone.

operationalization: Estimate median ages at thelarche and menarche and test whether both fall near fourteen and coincide with male puberty. A large shift of either event away from fourteen, or a wide gap between breast development and menarche, would fail the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: women's reproductive calendars, including age at first birth as a later marker

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility showing when childbearing begins in historical and modern populations

obstacles: First birth is later than menarche and thelarche.
Secular change means modern medians are a poor stand-in for a single ancient age without the historical series.
rationale: Menarche is widely studied, and fertility databases show the ages at which births begin, which bounds puberty from above. Breast development and first menses are separate events, and open surveys rarely store both Tanner stages. The age-fourteen conjunction is testable from compiled cohort studies for some populations and is not a single downloadable global table.

operationalization: Measure male fertility and births at ages under 21, and compare birth weight and congenital-anomaly rates by parental age. Any substantial fertility before 21 refutes infertility of the seed; a monotone penalty in offspring size or viability at young parental ages would support the second clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility rates, including ages under 21

candidate_datasets.name: WHO adolescent pregnancy fact sheet
candidate_datasets.role: births to adolescents and associated offspring risks

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: maternal age, birth weight and child outcomes in survey microdata

obstacles: Imperfect covers more outcomes than birth weight.
Paternal age under 21 is less complete than maternal age.
rationale: Age-specific fertility rates include the teenage years, so a claim that semen is infertile until 21 is directly testable. Survey and WHO summaries also relate young maternal age to birth weight and neonatal risk, which is the offspring clause. The infertility wording and the milder size-and-viability wording can fail independently, and both have public numbers.

operationalization: Pair semen consistency (thin versus granular or clotted) with subsequent offspring sex in a large series, holding count and motility fixed. A higher male fraction from granular samples and a higher female fraction from thin samples would support the claim.
obstacles: No public andrology table links semen consistency to offspring sex.
Small clinical series are confounded by the rest of the semen analysis.
rationale: Consistency and offspring sex are measurable, and a large paired series would discriminate the rule. Existing public fertility data do not carry both variables together. Scattered clinical notes are too small and confounded to confirm or refute the sex prediction.

operationalization: Score visible menstrual bleeding across birds, reptiles, fishes, viviparous quadrupeds and women. Bleeding confined to women would support the discharge clause; regular menstruation in other species would refute only women. Conversion of a residue into feathers, scales, hair or urine is a separate claim and needs a tracer the bleeding data do not supply.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode across vertebrates as context for which groups menstruate

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive accounts noting menstruation or its absence

obstacles: Residue converted into feathers or scales is not distinguished from simply lacking a discharge.
A few non-human mammals menstruate, and estrous bleeding can be mistaken for menstruation.
rationale: Who shows a menstrual discharge is an observable pattern, and species accounts plus comparative reviews cover it for many taxa. The further claim that the same material becomes feathers, scales, hair or urine has no measurement that separates it from the bare absence of bleeding. The distribution is partly testable; the conversion mechanism is not.

operationalization: From ultrasound series, record the gestational age of first fetal movement and the side of the uterus, split by fetal sex. Movement of males near day 40 on the right and females near day 90 on the left would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: Carnegie-stage ages and morphology, not the side of quickening

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: timetable of human embryonic and fetal movement

obstacles: Maternal quickening is later than the first movements seen on ultrasound.
Side of implantation by sex is not a field in open atlases.
rationale: First movement and fetal sex are routine ultrasound variables, and published series report when movement begins. Open embryo atlases fix ages and morphology and do not code uterine side by sex. The 40-versus-90-day and right-versus-left rules can be checked in those clinical series, which still have to be compiled.

operationalization: At Carnegie stages corresponding to about 40 days, measure crown-rump length against a large ant and score limb buds, genital tubercle or penis, and relative eye size. The claim fails if the embryo is far from that size or if a penis is not yet distinguishable.

candidate_datasets.name: Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: Carnegie-stage photographs and sizes around day 40

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: stage tables for length, limbs, eyes and external genitalia

obstacles: Staged embryos at this age are not labeled by genetic sex.
Penis versus undifferentiated genital tubercle is an anatomical judgment.
rationale: Open Carnegie atlases give length and external anatomy for the stage that falls near forty days. Size, limb visibility and relative eye size can be scored from those images. Sex-specific penis development is the clause the same stages are least able to support, because the external genitalia are still shared, and that is itself a result.

operationalization: Compare, by fetal sex, the gestational age at which defined organs reach a maturity criterion, and the distribution of gestational length at birth. Slower completion of parts in females and a higher share of female births at ten months would support the two clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: human developmental timetable against which sex differences would have to be shown

candidate_datasets.name: Eurostat
candidate_datasets.role: European birth statistics that include gestational age where the perinatal tables report it

obstacles: Sex-specific organogenesis timing is sparse in open atlases.
Ten months needs a declared lunar or calendar definition.
rationale: Gestational-age distributions by sex exist in perinatal statistics, which can test whether female births more often reach a ten-month term. A slower completion of parts in female embryos is a finer claim and is not a standard open table. The term clause is the one current civil-registration extracts can address; the organ-timing clause stays thinly measured.

operationalization: Compare within-species spread of gestation in humans with the spread in other mammals and other vertebrates, counting delayed implantation as real variation. The claim fails if other species have gestation ranges as wide as the human span from seven to eleven months, or if humans lack that span.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length across mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation and incubation across mammals, birds and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: Eurostat
candidate_datasets.role: European birth statistics that report gestational age, for the spread of human pregnancy length

obstacles: Many species are stored as a single gestation length, so within-species variance is under-reported.
Delayed implantation has to be counted as variation rather than dropped.
rationale: Human gestation is known to vary across months, and mammal and amniote databases record gestation for thousands of other species, including groups with delayed implantation and wide ranges. That comparison tests the claim that only humans vary. Single-value entries hide some variation, and the species with published ranges are already enough to test uniqueness.

operationalization: Using a pre-registered map of Aristotle's months onto weeks of gestation, estimate survival of infants born before that cutoff and at the seven-month boundary. Any survivors before the cutoff refute never; survival at the boundary with high morbidity would address the weakly clause.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO preterm birth fact sheet
candidate_datasets.role: gestational-age classes and survival of preterm infants

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Global Health Observatory
candidate_datasets.role: neonatal mortality indicators related to preterm birth

obstacles: Seven months can be read as lunar or calendar months.
Intensive care raises survival relative to ancient conditions, which still bears on under no circumstances.
rationale: WHO summaries report survival for very preterm and extremely preterm infants, which is the observation a universal never-survive claim has to meet. Mapping his months onto modern weeks is a declared assumption, and once it is fixed the survival figures confirm or refute the cutoff. Modern care changes the absolute rates and does not erase documented survival before a seven-month boundary.

operationalization: Compare survival of infants at a pre-registered eight-month gestational age in Egypt and Greece, in a period without modern neonatal intensive care if the historical claim is the target. Higher survival in Egypt and high mortality in Greece would support the geographic contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Global Health Observatory
candidate_datasets.role: country neonatal mortality, a coarse proxy for eight-month survival

obstacles: No ancient cohort records eight-month survival in Egypt versus Greece.
Modern hospital care removes the contrast the claim describes.
rationale: Country neonatal statistics exist, and they do not isolate an eight-month gestational class in classical populations. A modern Greece-Egypt comparison is a proxy dominated by medical care. The geographic claim as Aristotle states it lacks the cohort that would confirm or refute it.

operationalization: Find the maximum number of infants in one birth in civil-registration tables and documented case series. Any birth of six or more refutes five as the maximum; a ceiling of five in complete registries would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Eurostat
candidate_datasets.role: European birth statistics, including multiple deliveries

obstacles: Aggregate tables may top-code the highest multiplicities, so the extreme tail also depends on case series.
Assisted reproduction raises higher-order births relative to ancient conditions.
rationale: Civil-registration systems publish multiple-birth statistics, and a single reliable confinement of six or more refutes a maximum of five. Eurostat's birth tables are the open aggregate; case reports fill in the extreme tail. Assisted reproduction changes the frequency and is not required for the existence proof if unassisted higher-order births are also on record.

operationalization: Code whether females mate during an established pregnancy, for humans, horses, hares and a sample of other species. The claim stands if women and mares do so commonly, other species refuse, and hares are the superfetation exception.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mating and pregnancy accounts for horses, hares and other mammals

obstacles: Mating during pregnancy is not a standard trait column.
All other animals is far wider than existing ethograms.
rationale: Behavioral accounts document estrus, pregnancy and mating for horses, humans and hares, which covers the positive examples. A universal refusal by every other pregnant animal is not in any comparative table and fails as soon as further species with pregnancy mating are compiled. The test is feasible for the named species and open-ended for the universal clause.

operationalization: Estimate the age distribution of final menses and the oldest maternal ages at birth in natural-fertility populations. The claim stands if most women stop near 40, the tail reaches about 50, and births after 50 are absent.

candidate_datasets.name: Study of Women's Health Across the Nation
candidate_datasets.role: age at final menstrual period in a multi-ethnic cohort

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility through the forties and fifties

obstacles: SWAN is a modern cohort with a later menopause than the age of about forty.
Rare late births depend on how natural fertility is separated from assisted reproduction.
rationale: Cohort studies measure age at final menses, and the Human Fertility Database measures births by maternal age into the late reproductive years. Together they test the typical age, the upper tail near 50, and whether births occur beyond it. Modern menopause is later than forty in these series, which is a result rather than a barrier to the test.

operationalization: Estimate male fertility or documented paternity by age through 60 and 70. Continued paternity at 70 would support the upper example; a collapse of fertility well before 60 would refute the usual limit.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility, including paternal age in the series that record it

obstacles: Most fertility series are maternal age only.
Sexually competent is broader than documented paternity.
rationale: Where paternal age is recorded, births to men in their sixties and seventies test the upper ages directly. Many open fertility tables omit the father's age, so coverage is a subset of populations. Competence without a recorded birth is the clause those tables do not measure.

operationalization: Split the claim into congenital conditions and acquired marks. For named congenital traits, measure parent-child recurrence; for scars and pimples acquired in life, measure recurrence in children who did not share the injury. High recurrence of genetic conditions and none for scars would split the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: ClinVar
candidate_datasets.role: inherited congenital conditions with parent-child transmission

obstacles: Scars and acquired pimples are not in genetic databases.
Lame and blind mix injuries with heritable diseases.
rationale: ClinVar and pedigree studies catalogue congenital conditions that do recur in children, which tests the heritable half. Acquired scars have no corresponding public concordance table, and a hereditary reading of scars would require that table or a documented mechanism. The two halves do not stand or fall together.

operationalization: In three-generation pedigrees, count traits present in a grandparent and a grandchild and absent in the intervening parent. Recurring cases would support skip-generation resemblance; a pre-registered set of traits with no such cases would undermine the existential claim.

candidate_datasets.name: ClinVar
candidate_datasets.role: recessive and other pedigrees in which a phenotype reappears after a generation

obstacles: Open three-generation phenotype tables for ordinary resemblance are mostly restricted.
ClinVar covers medical traits, not facial resemblance in general.
rationale: Recessive pedigrees are a direct case of a trait visible in a grandparent and a grandchild and not in the parent, and those pedigrees are public for many conditions. General family resemblance, as distinct from a diagnosed trait, sits in cohort studies with controlled access. The existential genetic claim is testable; the everyday wording is broader than ClinVar.

operationalization: Compare staged embryos of a bird, a fish, a placental mammal and a placental shark on a pre-set list of early structures, and record where the nutritive cord attaches. The cord clause is supported by yolk-sac, uterine, or dual attachment in the groups named; the same-way clause needs those stages to match under the pre-set list.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish embryonic staging

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA chicken-embryo gene-expression atlas
candidate_datasets.role: chick embryonic stages and tissues

candidate_datasets.name: Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: human Carnegie stages for the viviparous comparison

obstacles: Develop in the same way is broad enough that early similarity and later difference both fit.
Placental-shark attachment is not in the model-organism atlases.
rationale: Public atlases make early development comparable across a fish, a bird and a human, and they show different nutritive attachments. That is the sharp part of the claim. A statement that all animals develop in the same way has no single mismatch that would retire it, because the stages one chooses change the answer.

operationalization: Record presentation at birth for humans and other viviparous animals, treating each species' usual presentation as the natural course. Universal head-first birth would support the claim; a species whose normal birth is tail-first, such as many cetaceans, would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: cetacean birth behavior, including usual presentation

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: birth descriptions for whales, dolphins and other mammals

obstacles: Natural course can be defined so that breech births do not count.
Presentation is well described for humans and cetaceans and sparse for most other mammals.
rationale: Usual presentation is recorded for humans and for whales and dolphins, and tail-first birth is the normal cetacean pattern in those accounts. That single group tests a claim about all animals. Livestock and wild mammals are less systematically tabulated, so the universal is vulnerable to the well-described exceptions and incompletely surveyed elsewhere.

operationalization: Count blood vessels in the umbilical cord of cattle, of a smaller mammal, and in the yolk-sac stalk of the chick. Four, two and one, in that order, would support the size rule; other stable counts would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: umbilical vessel counts in human and comparative developmental anatomy

candidate_datasets.name: Digimorph
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical imaging of vertebrate specimens where cords or yolk sacs are visible

obstacles: Published counts cover a handful of species, not a size series.
The chick uses paired vitelline vessels rather than a single umbilical cord.
rationale: Vessel number is a direct count, and veterinary and embryological descriptions give it for cattle, humans and the chick. Those descriptions are not a size-ordered trait table, so the three-step rule has to be assembled from them. The chick is the clearest potential mismatch because its yolk-sac circulation is not a single vessel.

operationalization: From eruption series, estimate the age of the first tooth and which tooth it is, and test whether warmer nurse's milk advances that age. Eruption in the seventh month, incisors first, would support the timing clauses; no milk-temperature effect would refute the last clause.

candidate_datasets.name: UNSW Embryology
candidate_datasets.role: timing of human primary-tooth development and eruption

obstacles: Milk temperature is not in eruption tables.
Seventh month needs a declared starting point from birth.
rationale: Deciduous eruption order and age are standard pediatric measurements, and open developmental references state that the incisors come first around the middle of the first year. The effect of the nurse's milk temperature is not in those tables. Timing and order can be checked; the milk clause cannot.

operationalization: In nationally representative surveys, estimate the rate of menses during breastfeeding versus after weaning, with time since birth held fixed. A large drop in bleeding while milk is produced, with a minority of exceptions, would support the general rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: breastfeeding and postpartum amenorrhea in survey microdata

obstacles: Survey amenorrhea is reported bleeding, not a hormone assay.
The moisture-in-one-direction explanation is not identified by the association alone.
rationale: Demographic and Health Surveys record breastfeeding and the return of menses for large samples of women. That is the general rule Aristotle states, including room for exceptions. The physiological story that moisture cannot flow in two directions at once is not what the survey association identifies, and the regularity itself is.

operationalization: No outcome distinguishes traces of gentleness, fierceness, courage, timidity or sagacity from their absence, because any behavioral difference can be called a trace, differing from humans in degree or by analogy.
obstacles: Psychical qualities and by analogy have no refuting observation.
Animal-personality scores would still count as traces under the wording.
rationale: The sentence asserts that most animals show some trace of human mental qualities, with the difference allowed to be either of degree or of analogy. Every measured behavior fits that wording, and no dataset result would show the traces to be absent. The claim is conceptual rather than a statement with a confirming and a refuting measurement.

operationalization: Place sponges, ascidians, sea anemones and sessile shellfish on current classifications of animals, plants and non-living things. A stable assignment to one kingdom would undermine cannot be assigned; the further claim that nature proceeds little by little from the lifeless has no separate metric in those names.

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: classification of sponges, ascidians, anemones and sessile molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Taxonomy
candidate_datasets.role: placement of the same intermediate forms in Metazoa

obstacles: Nature proceeds little by little is a scheme, not a measurement.
Modern kingdoms answer the assignment question and leave the continuum claim open.
rationale: The named intermediate organisms now have stable taxonomic placements, which tests the clause that they cannot be assigned to one side or the other. A gradual passage from lifeless things to animals is not fixed by those placements. Taxonomy resolves the examples; it does not operationalize the whole scala.

operationalization: Proxy intelligence and memory by brain size or by documented performance, and parental association by weaning age or time to independence, then test the correlation with body size and phylogeny controlled. A positive partial association would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: weaning age and age at maturity as association-time proxies

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: weaning age and life-history timing across mammals

obstacles: Weaning age ends nutritional dependence and not social life with the young.
Brain size and memory tests are separate compilations and are confounded by body size.
rationale: Duration of offspring dependence is tabulated widely. Intelligence and memory are not columns in those tables, so the test uses a proxy and inherits the proxy's confounds. A correlation of weaning with brain size can be assembled and would still leave memory, as distinct from brain size, weakly measured.

operationalization: For sea turtles, crocodiles, hippopotamus, seals, freshwater turtles and frogs, record respiratory organ and survival during forced submersion, plus whether they breed on or near land. Death or distress without access to air, and terrestrial or shoreline breeding, would support the claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: respiration and breeding habitat for turtles, crocodiles, hippos and seals

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: frog respiration and breeding sites

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: sea-turtle and seal biology, including air breathing and haul-out or nesting

obstacles: Some turtles and frogs exchange gas through cloaca or skin and endure long submersion.
Drown is a graded outcome, not a single submersion time.
rationale: Lung breathing, the need to reach air, and breeding on or near land are documented for each named group in open species accounts. Those accounts also record cutaneous or cloacal gas exchange, which qualifies how quickly a frog or turtle is distressed. The named list is small enough to score species by species.

operationalization: For dolphins, confirm lungs and air breathing, time to suffocation in nets, survival in air, and whether sleep occurs with the blowhole above water. Each clause fails on its own measurement: gills instead of lungs, prolonged survival underwater in a net, immediate death in air, or submerged sleep without access to air.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries
candidate_datasets.role: dolphin respiration, entanglement and surface behavior

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: lung anatomy, surfacing and parental behavior of dolphins

obstacles: Time-to-suffocation and time-alive-in-air are reported as observations more often than as a single trial table.
Sleep posture is described for a subset of species.
rationale: Lungs, entanglement asphyxia, haul-out or deck survival and surface breathing during rest are standard items in dolphin species accounts. The anatomical clause is settled by dissection and by those accounts together. Durations and sleep posture are quantitative details inside the same literature, with fewer formal trials than the lung claim.

operationalization: Separate two clauses: gilled fishes pass water over the gills, and blowhole animals take in water while feeding rather than as their respiratory medium. Physiology then has to show that gill flow functions to cool the blood rather than to exchange gases, for example by survival in warm oxygenated water versus cold oxygen-poor water.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: gill and respiratory-mode records for fishes

obstacles: Cooling versus oxygen uptake is not a FishBase field.
The purpose clause needs experiments that are scattered in physiology papers.
rationale: Presence of gills versus a blowhole is anatomical and is widely recorded, including the point that cetaceans breathe air. The claim that water is taken in to cool the blood is a function that gas-exchange experiments can in principle separate from oxygenation. Those experiments are not assembled as a comparative dataset, so the function remains weakly tested.

operationalization: For each candidate identification of the cordylus, record gills, lungs and terrestrial locomotion, and test uniqueness against other amphibians. The claim stands only if one animal has gills, lacks lungs, walks on land and is the only such animal.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: respiration and habitat of newts, salamanders and other amphibians with gills

obstacles: Cordylus may be a newt larva, a salamander or an aquatic proteid.
Several amphibians have external gills, and larvae also have developing lungs.
rationale: AmphibiaWeb records gills, lungs and habitat for the animals that might be the cordylus. Uniqueness and the combination of no lungs plus land walking can be checked once the name is fixed, and the plausible identifications do not share that combination. The limit is the name, not the absence of amphibian life-history data.

operationalization: Score secondary sexual traits before and after castration in a pre-set list of species, and separately test whether embryo sex tracks the size of an early organ rather than chromosomal or environmental sex determination. A shift toward female form after removal of the gonad would support the castration clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of sexual dimorphism and, where described, effects of castration

obstacles: Castration outcomes are in livestock studies more than in a trait database.
Mammalian sex is not decided by the size of an embryonic organ, and that contrast is in developmental papers.
rationale: The castration example is a concrete before-and-after comparison, documented for several domestic species and not gathered in one open table. The general claim that any minute organ can reshape the whole animal is too open to fail. Embryonic sex determination by organ size is a distinct mechanism and is addressed by developmental studies rather than by the castration records.

operationalization: Lower an empty thin wax vessel into seawater for 24 hours and measure the volume and salinity of any water inside. A drinkable yield would support the claim; an empty vessel or a saline yield would refute it.
obstacles: Ocean salinity archives do not run the wax-vessel procedure.
No public replication series with volume and salinity was located.
rationale: The procedure and the pass-fail measurement are fully specified. Public salinity data describe seawater and do not substitute for water recovered inside a wax vessel. Resolving the prediction requires a reported replication, which is not available as a dataset.

operationalization: In diet records with identified prey, code intraspecific predation for fishes and for mullets, and compare the conger with other species. The universal fails if well-studied species have no conspecific prey; the mullet exception fails if mullets eat conspecifics.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet items, including conspecifics where recorded, for fishes and mullets

obstacles: Missing cannibalism records are not evidence of absence.
Diet studies over-represent commercial species.
rationale: FishBase food-item records include conspecific prey for many species, which can refute a ban and can check mullets and the conger. Most species lack a diet study thorough enough to treat a zero as real. The exception and the especially ravenous clause are testable in the studied subset; the word all is not.

operationalization: In dissections or scans, measure whether an esophagus separates the mouth from the stomach across a phylogenetic sample of fishes. A stomach immediately behind the mouth and no esophagus would support the claim; a distinct gullet in ordinary teleosts would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: morphological notes on the alimentary tract where species accounts include them

candidate_datasets.name: Digimorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT imagery of fish specimens for mouth, esophagus and stomach position

obstacles: Esophagus presence is described in anatomical papers more often than as a FishBase field.
Digimorph includes few fish species.
rationale: Presence or absence of a gullet is a dissection finding, and comparative anatomy covers it for many fishes. Open databases hold that fact unevenly: species accounts sometimes describe the gut, and scanned specimens are few. A short esophagus can be scored as present or absent under a pre-set length rule, which is enough to test the universal in a compiled sample.
